## Paper

## Abstract

The ferroelectric oxide LaTaO4, with a layered perovskite-related structure, exhibits a reversible temperature-dependent phase transition between its low-temperature paraelectric and high-temperature ferroelectric states. Herein, using in situ three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED) with atomic-resolution, we resolve the structural evolution of LaTaO4 nanocrystals across four distinct phases during sequential heating treatment (300-500 K). Beyond ab initio structure determination of the known monoclinic (m-LaTaO4) and orthorhombic (o-LaTaO4) phases, we unravel: (i) a, previously undetected, intermediate phase (m'-LaTaO4) with a shorter c-axis transiently stabilized at around 372 K, arising from tilting of TaO6 octahedra; (ii) an incommensurately modulated phase (IC-o-LaTaO4) with a modulation vector q ≈ (0.4669, 0, 0) through a combination of 3D ED and high-resolution electron microscopy imaging. The real-time tracking reveals three first-order phase transitions governed by synergetic Ta-O bond distortion dynamics. These findings establish a hierarchical phase transition model that reconciles previous studies and these single nanocrystal observations.

---

## Introduction

Ferroelectric materials1 exhibit a spontaneous net polarizationP, the direction of which is reversibly switchable under an external applied electric field. Consequently, these material s have garnered substantial interest for capacitor, sensor, actuator, and memory device applications. Ferroelectric materials can be formed via a phase transition from paraelectric phases under specific conditions, which is typically accomplished by symmetry breaking. Although the most widely-used ferroelectric materials adopt the perovskite structure, a wide range of other ferroelectrics exist within layered perovskite-like structures including Ruddlesden-Popper, Dion-Jacobson, Aurivillius and Carpy-Galy families.2,3 The latter can be derived from the perovskite (ABX3) structure by cleaving along the [110] plane and incorporation of additional anions, giving rise to the homologous series with general formula AnBnX3n+2, where n represents the number of perovskite blocks between cleaved planes. Within this Carpy-Galy4 family, the n = 4 materials Sr2Nb2O75 and La2Ti2O76,7 aroused significant attention in ferroelectric and piezoelectric research, due to their very high operating temperatures. Notably however, LaTaO48-12is the sole ferroelectric oxide n = 2 member in this family (although CeTaO4 and PrTaO4 also adopt the Carpy-Galy structure they exclusively form only in the non-polar polymorph); LaNbO4 and all other lanthanide (Ln) tantalates and niobates with ABX4 stoichiometry adopted either the non-perovskite-related fergusonite or scheelite structures.13-15 LaTaO4 is of particular interest as it shares structural similarities with the prototypical ferroelectric fluoride analogue, BaMnF4,16 which exhibits a stable nonpolar monoclinic P21/c phase (m-phase) at room temperature and a stable polar orthorhombic Cmc21 phase at high temperature.17,18 In previous studies of the phase transitions of LaTaO4,17,19 an incommensurately modulated structure was identified between the low temperature m-phase and the high temperature o-phase, accompanied by dielectric anomalies during heating and cooling.

Previous studies on crystal structures and phase transitions of LaTaO4 mainly rely on powder X-ray or neutron diffraction.8,20 However, three-dimensional reciprocal information was projected to one dimension in these techniques, leading to peak overlaps and potential oversight of subtle reflection signals in background noises. These limitations hinder differentiation between similar structures and increase the risk of missing key features. Three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED)21,22 is an emerging method developed in the past two decades, which has been applied to structure analysis of various materials including inorganic minerals, proteins, crystalline porous materials, etc.23-26 In particular, in situ 3D ED affords the capability of probing not only crystal structures under various environments, e.g. cryogenic temperatures, electric fields, in situ heating, and in gas and liquid environments, but also the dynamic structure evolution under external stimuli.27-29

Here, we utilised in situ 3D ED to track the successive phase transitions of LaTaO4 nanocrystals during thermal cycling. The temperature-dependent structural evolution was resolved through the analysis of 3D reciprocal lattices. In addition to the three previously reported phases, a previously unreported intermediate monoclinic phase, denoted as m'-LaTaO4 phase, was identified between the monoclinic and incommensurate orthorhombic phases in some nanocrystals. Through ab initio structural solutions, we characterised all crystalline phases and established their relationships. By combining 3D ED data with high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) imaging, we elucidated the incommensurate modulation structure including its modulation vector, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of various atomic-level structures in LaTaO4.

---

## Results

In situ heating 3D ED of LaTaO4

In previous reports, three phases were identified in LaTaO4 during its sequential phase transitions: a monoclinic phase at room temperature (m-LaTaO4), an orthorhombic phase at high temperature (o-LaTaO4), and an intermediate incommensurately modulated orthorhombic phase (IC-o-LaTaO4). The correlation between the m-LaTaO4 and o-LaTaO4 unit cells can be described by a transformation matrix:

(ao) = (0 2 0) · (am)
(bo) = (0 0 1) · (bm) (1)
(co) = (1 1 0) · (cm)

where ao, bo, co represent the unit cell parameters of o-LaTaO4 and am, bm, cm represent those of m-LaTaO4. The [001] zone axis of o-LaTaO4, denoted as [001]o, is equivalent to the [010] zone axis of m-LaTaO4, denoted as [010]m. For clarification, the subscript of the zone axis indicates the corresponding phase.

In this work, the typical crystal structures of m-LaTaO4 (a = 7.67 Å, b = 5.67 Å, and c = 7.94 Å, β = 101.57°, space group P21/c) and o-LaTaO4 (a = 4.05 Å, b = 15.11 Å, and c = 5.80 Å, space group Cmc21) were successfully determined using 3D ED data (Supplementary Fig. 1 and 2 and Supplementary Table 1). To investigate the phase transition behaviour of LaTaO4 during progressive heating, an in situ heating 3D ED experiment was carefully designed and conducted (Fig. 1), so that 3D ED datasets were collected at preset temperatures with a fixed heating rate of 5 K/min (Fig. 1a) from multiple LaTaO4 nanocrystals (Fig. 1b), followed by an equilibration period of 5 mins at each temperature.

3D ED datasets (Fig. 2a-c) were firstly collected at 300 K, from which a monoclinic unit cell with parameters a = 7.63 Å, b = 5.63 Å, and c = 7.92 Å, β = 101.09° was determined, consistent with previously reported m-LaTaO4. However, analysis of 2D slices from the 3D ED data revealed the presence of numerous diffraction spots with h0l (l = 2n+1), which contradicts the systematic absences expected for the widely reported space group P21/c. Given the composition of heavy atoms (La, Ta) and the high density, this observation is likely attributed to strong dynamical scattering effects. This interpretation is supported by a consistent intensity difference observed between h0l reflections with l = 2n and l = 2n+1 indices. From a property perspective, the assignment of the centrosymmetric P21/c space group remains consistent with the well-documented paraelectric behaviour of m-LaTaO4. The observed reflection conditions were summarised as h0l: l = 2n; 00l: l = 2n; 0k0: k = 2n, shown in Supplementary Fig. 3. During heating, SAED patterns along a fixed orientation of the same crystal were recorded with 0.5 s exposure time. Representative SAED patterns at 360, 380 and 400 K are shown in Fig. 1c-e. At 360 K, SAED patterns displayed sharp diffraction spots from both zero-order Laue zone (ZOLZ) and first-order Laue zone (FOLZ), indexed to the [1̅20] of m-LaTaO4. It is worth noting that some diffraction spots, such as 003 and 003̅, should be systematically absent based on the reported space group P21/c but weak spots are present in the experimental SAED pattern (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 4). This indicates the existence of strong dynamical scattering, which corroborates with the emergence of h0l (l = 2n+1) reflections in 3D ED datasets.

A line profile was extracted from the diffraction pattern along (001̅) direction (marked by the dotted yellow rectangle in Fig. 1c-e), from 214 to 216̅ reflections (Fig. 1f). By recording SAED patterns along the identical orientation of the same nanocrystal during heating, the evolution of diffraction spots could be tracked (Supplementary Video 1 and 2). Fig. 1g and h show the change in intensity of the reflections shown in Fig. 1f during the heating with an interval of 1 K. No obvious change was observed from 300 to 368 K. In this range of temperature, the unit cells determined from 3D ED datasets remain the same as m-LaTaO4. When temperature was increased to approx. 372 K, the nanocrystal underwent a first change. In the range 368 ~ 380 K, the intensities of strong diffraction spots display a visible fluctuation at around 372 K and gradually stabilize at 380 K. Moreover, the 216̅ reflection (marked with an arrow in Fig. 1g) shows a slight shift. Subsequent 3D ED data analysis at 380 K showed significant intensity reduction in h0l (l ≠ 2n) reflections versus room-temperature data (Supplementary Fig. 5). Since two 3D ED datasets are collected from the same particle, the changes in reflection intensities and positions indicate a potential phase transition.

It is worth noting that the changes in intensity of many other reflections are not so prominent. After careful analysis of the 3D ED dataset at 380 K, a monoclinic phase with parameters a = 7.78 Å, b = 5.65 Å, c = 3.97 Å, and β = 100.94° with a space group of P21 could be determined, denoted as m'-LaTaO4 (Fig. 2d-f). However, this intermediate m'-phase is not very stable and only appears in a narrow temperature range. In many cases, m- and m'-phases might coexist in LaTaO4 nanocrystals. Notably, the m'-phase exhibits such subtle structural differences that it remains undetectable in conventional powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) and neutron diffraction (PND). This limitation arises from two fundamental factors: Firstly, the pronounced overlap of diffraction peaks between the m- and m'-phases leads to statistical averaging of their respective signals in PXRD/PND patterns, effectively obscuring the weaker m'-phase signatures during analysis. Secondly, the m'-LaTaO4 likely exists only at the nanoscale or within localised structural domains, making it inherently challenging to observe through other characterisation techniques.

As the temperature continues to increase from 380 K, the intensities of diffraction spots remain stable until the second phase transition occurs, from the m'-phase to IC-o phase, at ca. 389 K. In addition to changes in reflection intensities, the positions of 214 and 214̅ reflections also shift (marked with yellow arrows in Fig. 1h). Analysis of in situ 3D ED data at 400 K reveals an orthorhombic unit cell with incommensurate modulation (Fig. 2g-i), where the basic cell parameters (a = 3.95 Å, b = 14.58 Å and c = 5.69 Å) agree well with the reported o-LaTaO4. Distinct ‘zig-zag’ satellite spots appear along the (001) direction with a modulation vector q ≈ (0.4669, 0, 0) in 3D reciprocal space, consistent with the previous study by Howieson et al.17

As the temperature continues to increase to ca. 394 ~ 400 K, the diffraction pattern shows a final change, with variations in reflection intensity only (Fig. 1e). Subsequent 3D ED data (Fig. 2j-l) confirms the formation of the high-temperature orthorhombic phase, o-LaTaO4. The unit cell parameters could be determined as a = 3.92 Å, b = 14.41 Å and c = 5.61 Å (at 500 K), with the space group Cmc21. Notably, these phase transition temperatures (389 or 394 K) are lower than widely-reported ones (~ 440 K8,17). Given the non- negligible volume changes among different phases, from 333.61 Å3 (m-LaTaO4 @300 K), 335.76 Å3 (2×m'-LaTaO4 @380 K), 327.52 Å3 (IC-o-LaTaO4 @400 K) to 316.32 Å3 (o-LaTaO4 @500 K), a possible origin of the change in transition temperatures (Tc) value is strain, that the expansion in unit cell volume during heating may have effect on lattice strains, resulting in a decrease of Tc. The dependence of Tc on unit cell volume have been reported in perovskite such as LaCoO330 And the Tc of ferroelectric (CnH2n+1NH3)2(CH3NH3)n-1PbnBr3n+1 could be decreased by the expansion of unit cells.31 Another possible answer could be the size effect of nanoparticles. Zhong et al.32 hypothesised and validated that Tc would drop as the size of ferroelectric nanoparticles decreases using a Landau phenomenological theory. Lyberatos et al.33 proposed that the Curie temperature of L1o-FePt would decrease as the size decreases based on simulations using a Monte Carlo model.

Structure analysis of LaTaO4 phases

In situ 3D ED datasets of all phases (m-LaTaO4, m'-LaTaO4, IC-o-LaTaO4 (main reflections)and o-LaTaO4) were processed using XDS34 software. Ab initio structure solutions were obtained using direct methods in SIR2019,35 followed by structure refinements using SHELXL36 in OLEX237. Crystallographic details of selected 3D ED datasets at 300, 340, 380, 400, 440, 480 and 500 K are provided in Supplementary Table 2. Structural comparisons of m-LaTaO4, m'-LaTaO4 and IC-o-LaTaO4 (Fig. 3) reveal that, apart from minor La position variations, the main difference of these structures lies in the arrangement of twin TaO6 octahedral blocks (TO). In the m-phase, TaO6 octahedra exhibit an overall out-of-phase tilt around [001]m while in both the m'- and o-phases the octahedral tilting is in-phase along the equivalent axis, [001]m' and [100]o, respectively. As a result, m-LaTaO4 has two types of twin TaO6 octahedra stacked alternately, TOm1 and TOm2 (marked with arrows), along the [001] (or [100]o) direction whilst m'-LaTaO4 and o-LaTaO4 have only one type (TOm' and TOo respectively). The measured angles of Ta–O–Ta (Δθ) in these structures show deviations from 180° (the un-tilted parent Cmcm structure): ΔθTOm1 = 38.462°, ΔθTOm2 = -38.462°, ΔθTOm' = 35.54° and ΔθTOo = 33.34°, respectively (the absolute value of ΔθTOm1 and ΔθTOm2 are equal because of the c-centring symmetry of P21/c). This progressive Δθ change indicates that from m-LaTaO4 to m'-LaTaO4, the TO6 octahedra rotate, with one TaO6 block TOm2 rotating anticlockwise, and the other block TOm1 rotating clockwise, resulting in the alignment of TOm' and TOm' along [001]m. And the overall transition from m-LaTaO4 to o-LaTaO4 has the tendency to a higher degree of octahedral alignment towards an ideal (un-tilted) Cmcm structure. This trend is corroborated by temperature-dependent Δθ analysis (Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 3). Data merging could improve the data completeness but shows little changes on the structure refinement statistics in our cases (Supplementary Table 4).

Regarding the phase transformation from m'-LaTaO4 to IC-o-LaTaO4, a comparison between m'-LaTaO4 and the averaged IC-o-LaTaO4 was conducted, as illustrated in Fig. 3b. Differences could be seen along [010]m', where no obvious rotations of TaO6 octahedra could be identified, but an overall shift of the n = 2 TaO6 layers and La ions along the [001] direction was found. Although the shift is small, ca. 0.36a of the unit cell (~ 1.44 Å), it induces the alignment of La and TaO6 blocks along the [010] direction, resulting in an orthogonal arrangement that drives the structure to a different phase of LaTaO4.

However, mere consideration of only the main reflections does not completely represent the exact structure of IC-o-LaTaO4 as satellite spots were excluded in the structure determination. To further investigate the superstructures, multiple datasets of m'-LaTaO4 and IC-o-LaTaO4 from several repeated experiments were analysed. For IC-o-LaTaO4, accounting for weak diffraction spots revealed an incommensurately modulated supercell along the a-axis. The q vectors from all IC-o-LaTaO4 phases have been determined and summarised (Supplementary Table 5). Furthermore, after introducing a modulation vector in data processing of 3D ED datasets using PETS2 (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 7a),38 the intensity of satellite spots could be integrated, generating a (3+1)D reflection file rather than a standard hkl file. The 0th slices of IC-o-LaTaO4 in hk0m and h0lm are shown in Supplementary Fig. 8. The first-order satellites could be seen in the IC-o-LaTaO4 dataset, but second-order satellite spots are absent, hence only m = 1 is considered. Similarly, the reflections suffer from strong dynamical scattering, by considering the variation of reflection conditions, the reflection conditions could be summarised as hklm: h+k = 2n, and h0lm: l+m = 2n. The reflection conditions are compatible with superspace group Cmc21(α00)0s0, C2cm(α00)ss0 (Ama2(00g)0ss in the standard setting) and Cmcm(α00)0s0. Cmcm(α00)0s0 was excluded, as its basic space group Cmcm is centrosymmetric, which is incompatible with the widely reported ferroelectricity nature of the high temperature LaTaO4 phase.8,9 For the non-centrosymmetric alternatives, C2cm(α00)ss0 was not selected because its symmetry forbids the modulation of z, which precludes any modulated displacement functions along z in the incommensurately modulated model. Such constraints are incompatible with the tilting-dominated incommensurate modulation. In addition, the C2cm symmetry would impose strict constraints on the local atomic geometry. Therefore, the non-centrosymmetric space group Cmc21(α00)0s0 is selected for the incommensurate modulation. The reflection condition with index could be seen in Supplementary Fig. 9. The structure refinement workflow contains: (1) ab initio solution and refinement using only main reflections; (2) reprocessing reflection data including satellite spots; (3) kinematical structure refinement in JANA202039 by introducing a modulation vector q = (0.4669, 0, 0) and superspace group Cmc21(α00)0s0 (Supplementary Fig. 7b). The refinement statistics are summarised in Supplementary Table 6. The finalised model could be seen in Fig. 4b and c, and the de Wolff sections could be seen in Supplementary Fig. 10.

In the refined incommensurately modulated superstructure model of IC-o-LaTaO4, Ta, O and La atoms exhibit positional variations, resulting in a tilting of TaO6 octahedra and a minor displacement of La (Supplementary Video 3 and 4). The tilting of TaO6 is accompanied by minor deformations, which does not appear to be symmetry-dictated. To give a clear presentation, we built a superstructure model with 22×a (Fig. 4d), in which two types of TaO6 blocks with different orientations were identified. These blocks are alternatively connected and exhibit subtle differences in oxygen displacement magnitude, with variations manifesting a long-range modulation period. To display this structural feature, a colour contrast gradient is introduced in Fig. 4d depending on the extent of oxygen position variation. As the oxygen atoms vary in their positions, there are always regions where unit cells of type A and B show more similar structures. This similarity is followed by a gradual deviation between two types until reaching regions with maximum structural difference. However, if we further extend the scale of the model, one can easily find that the periods are not commensurate. This is where the incommensurate modulation originates. This principle aligns with the formation mechanism of incommensurate structures proposed in our previous study, i.e. that the partial ordering of two or more different blocks is the origin for the formation of the incommensurate structures.17

JANA software has been widely used to determine incommensurately modulated crystal structures, mainly utilizing powder or single-crystal X-ray diffraction and powder neutron diffraction data.40-43 In common cases, electron microscopy primarily provides SAED and HRTEM images from limited orientations. Recently, more exemplar research has been reported on the structure refinement of incommensurately modulated structures using 3D ED, PED, etc.21,44-47 Building upon the ongoing development of 3D ED methodologies, this work presents a further application case, demonstrating its utility for refining an incommensurately modulated structure upon in situ heating scenario. Notably, 3D ED has exhibited a strong capability in identifying modulated structures by offering the advantage of not only free rotation in 3D reciprocal space but also accurate indexing during determining the modulation vectors. Conventionally, determining modulation vectors through either real space or reciprocal space by electron microscopy is usually time-consuming and lacks accuracy. This is because structure modulation determination requires a large number of images taken from different orientations, all of which require accurate indexing prior to satellite spots analysis. Furthermore, SAED patterns represent 2D sections of reciprocal space. The interpretation of satellite spots or weak superlattice reflections could be insufficient due to its limited orientation, making it difficult in correctly determining the incommensurate modulation or other superstructures in these materials. In contrast, 3D ED datasets provide structural information in 3D reciprocal space, enabling unrestricted rotation of reconstructed 3D data and 2D section until the correct modulation vector is identified. In addition, with the exploitation of data processing software, e.g. PETS2,38 the modulation vectors can be reliably determined and refined.

The incommensurate structure was further confirmed through high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) imaging. Fig. 5a-d shows a representative HRTEM image taken along the [001]o direction with its corresponding fast Fourier transform (FFT) pattern and electron diffraction pattern. Analysis of satellite spots observed in the FFT and electron diffraction gives the modulation vector q ≈ (0.4624, 0, 0), which is close to that from 3D ED data (0.4669, 0, 0). A line profile along the [100]o direction (Fig. 5e) reveals prominent intensity variations superimposed on the periodic lattice fringes. Two distinct periods exhibiting wave-like modulations are identified (marked in blue for period 1 and red for period 2 in Fig. 5e). By selecting main Fourier coefficients or satellites in the FFT data and performing inverse Fourier transformation, two different images were obtained (middle and bottom left in Fig. 5e). The corresponding line profile (blue curve in Fig. 5e) of only the main reflections presents an overall even distribution whilst the line profile of the satellite reflections (red curve in Fig. 5e) resembles a harmonic wave, with a ca. 6.5×a period. This abnormal contrast difference originates from atomic-scale structural modulations involving La atomic displacements and cooperative TaO6 octahedra tilting. Moreover, HRTEM observations show good agreement with the proposed structure model (Supplementary Fig. 11), that alternating type A and type B domains exhibit characteristic contrast variations over extended length scales. From the full scale filtered HRTEM images with the FFTs in Supplementary Fig. 12, the wavelike patterns, which indicate the incommensuration in the LaTaO4 structure, are distributed across the whole specimen area.

As a sequential work following the study of IC-o-LaTaO4 carried out by Howieson et al.,17 a comparison with the current work can be made. While no unit cell can be strictly defined for incommensurate structures, an expanded supercell with ordered building blocks (“slabs”) approaching the incommensurate structure serves as a conceptual framework for understanding structure formation.48,49 Unlike the “slab” incommensurate model, which assumes partial ordering of building blocks M (6×a/2) and N (5×a/2) based on SAED and HRTEM observations, this work constructs a single-crystal-level structural description. Specifically, we propose a structure model with quantified atomic position approximation rather than “slab” subunit hypothesis. Meanwhile, differing from conventional refinement of a standard database structure using PND data, this study conducted ab initio structure solution, together with structure refinement using 3D ED data, enabling improved approximation of local structural realism.

Nonetheless, despite the differences, the models in the current work are not at odds with those previously reported, but instead complement the understanding of the incommensurate modulation in LaTaO4. The modulation vector q of IC-o-LaTaO4 is close to the reported vector (0.456, 0, 0), exhibiting consistent SAED patterns along the [001]o direction. HRTEM images reveal two alternating intensity periods with wave-like characteristics (top right in Fig. 5e), suggesting that at least two building blocks contribute to the modulated structure in LaTaO4. It is important to note that both “slab” and our models are approximations of the real structure, as satellite spot intensity arises from atomic displacements across hundreds of unit cells.

Overall, the benefits of in situ heating 3D ED reflect in many extents, that upon progressive heating, it is possible to track the crystal structure evolution and obtain a realistic structure under different environments, effectively capturing phase transition behaviour of LaTaO4 nanocrystals. Moreover, the rapid 3D ED data collection makes it possible to detect subtle changes in structures, enabling discovery of transient phases such as the potential intermediate phase, m'-LaTaO4. In this work, the phase transitions and structural evolution of LaTaO4 were investigated using in situ 3D ED coupled with HRTEM imaging. Upon heating the specimen from 300 K to 500 K, the monoclinic phase (m-LaTaO4) underwent a phase transition to an intermediate phase (m'-LaTaO4) at approximately 372 K. Such a phase transition involves a tilting of TO6 blocks to align with TOm1, generating the intermediate phase structurally analogous to m-LaTaO4 but with a unit cell halved in c. Subsequently, the octahedral layers undergo a shift along the [001]m' direction during the transition to an incommensurately modulated orthorhombic phase (IC-o-LaTaO4) with a modulation along the a-axis and a modulation vector q ≈ (0.4669, 0, 0). A final transition at approximately 394 K yielded the fully ordered orthorhombic phase (o-LaTaO4). The crystal structures of m-LaTaO4, m'-LaTaO4 and the averaged IC-o-LaTaO4 phases were resolved ab initio. Based on 3D ED data and HRTEM image analysis, an incommensurately modulated model of IC-o-LaTaO4 was proposed. The methodology demonstrated in the present work enables investigation of phase transitions with subtle structural changes in many other solid materials.

## Methods

Material Synthesis

The m-LaTaO4 specimen was prepared as a polycrystalline powder according to previous literature17 and used as prepared without further purification. A standard synthesis procedure involves: Reagents are dried for 1 hour before use—La2O3 at 1000 °C and Ta2O5 at 600 °C. Stoichiometric quantities of the oxides are mixed via milling at 600 rpm for 1 hour in a planetary ball mill, then pressed into pellets 10 ~ 13 mm in diameter using either 1 tonne uniaxial pressure or 200 MPa isostatic pressure. The pellets are subsequently annealed at 1650 °C for 6 hours.

In situ heating 3D ED experiment

Sample preparation. The original m-LaTaO4 specimen was used in the in situ heating experiment. The sample was crushed and dispersed in anhydrous ethanol. The dispersed sample was dropped onto an in situ chip (Fusion Select by Protochips Co. Ltd.) with a 3×3 mesh and left to allow the complete evaporation of ethanol. It should be noted that the amount of dispersed sample was low to avoid blocking of the mesh apertures.

In situ system setup. The heating procedure was controlled by an in situ heating system, which consists of a heater, an in situ specimen holder (Fusion Select: E-FHDC-VO) and a controlling terminal (controlling software Fusion installed in a PC). The in situ holder was connected to the heater and the controlling terminal. The software checks the connection between in situ chip, heater and the controlling system, and the ‘pass’ feedback indicates the in situ system is ready to perform the experiment. For each in situ chip, a calibration file was provided by the manufacturer in order to calibrate the controller electricity parameters under different temperatures and ramping rates. The calibration file was imported to the controlling software before experiment.

TEM setup. The in situ experiment was performed on JEOL JEM-F200 microscope with an ASI Cheetah 1800 camera and a RIO-16 camera. The microscope, with an acceleration voltage of 200 kV, was aligned before experiment.

In situ heating 3D ED experiment design. The temperature was set to 300 K at the beginning of experiment, then increased with a constant rate of 5 K/min, and paused at 300, 340, 380, 400, 440, 480 and finally 500 K to collect 3D ED data (Figure 1). Temperature stabilization for ca. 5 mins was applied before 3D ED data collection. One single crystal was tracked and its SAED patterns were recorded during the heating procedure.

In situ 3D ED data collection. The in situ 3D ED datasets were collected using the ASI-Cheetah 1800 camera combined with a modified INSTAMATIC data collection software.22,28,50 The continuous rotation electron diffraction (cRED) method was used in data collection and an exposure time of either 0.3 s or 0.5 s was used. Due to the dimension of holder, the collection range was -25 ~ 25°.

HRTEM imaging. HRTEM images were taken with a Gatan RIO-16 detector equipped on a JEOL JEM-F200 transmission electron microscope, operating at 200 kV.

Data processing, structural solution and refinement

3D ED reconstruction. The data processing was performed using PETS238 software, including signal extraction and 3D reconstruction. The reflection diameter for peak search is 10 pixels and I/sigma for 20. The original modulated vector was determined and refined as q = (0.4669, 0.0028, -0.0006). The LaTaO4 phases were recognised, their unit cells and the superspace groups were determined using the reconstructed 3D ED data and reciprocal sections generated by PETS2. The frame geometry and reflection profile were also optimised before integration.

Intensity integration. The intensity integration of diffraction spots was conducted by an XDS software for ab initio structural solution. For the incommensurate phase, the determined unit cell and space group were imported into XDS to extract the diffraction information for structural solution of the basic unit cell and refinement of the periodic crystal structure. Besides, data with the modulation vector with maximum satellite order of 1 were integrated and finalised using an integrate profile for intensity estimation in PETS2 in order to refine the modulated structure.

Structural solution and refinement. The initial structural solutions of m-LaTaO4, m'-LaTaO4 and o-LaTaO4 were obtained using direct methods in SIR201935 and refined using a SHELXL36 program in OLEX237. The averaged structure of IC-o-LaTaO4 was also obtained by this means. To gain an incommensurately modulated structure, a satellite-containing (3+1)D reflection file processed by PETS2 was imported to the refinement of the averaged IC-o-LaTaO4 structure using JANA202039. A least-squares method was used for refinement.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript describes the analysis of phases and phase transitions arising upon heating of LaTaO4. The information was obtained by in-situ heating of the material and collecting 3D ED data at several temperatures.
The basic idea of the manuscript is interesting and worthy of pursuing. It is not new (see e.g. Kamba et al., https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.95.174103), but, to my knowledge, it has not yet been performed to such an extent in terms of temperature range and number of phases. The experiments also seem to have been performed carefully, and the basic results, in general, appear reliable.
The weakest point of the manuscript is the amount of information (or rather the lack of it) on the incommensurate phase. It is claimed to be one of the highlights of the manuscript, but the presentation suffers from a number of flaws.
First, the claim that this is the first case of the incommensurate structure refinement against 3D ED data is almost comically wrong. I know that it is hard to keep track of all the literature, but if the authors want to make such a bold claim, they should do at least a basic literature search to verify the claim is correct. Had they done so, they would have found that refinement of incommensurate structures from 3D ED data is quite common, using both the kinematical approach (which seems to be the approach used in this manuscript) and the more advanced dynamical refinement. Already, the review by Gemmi et al. (2019), cited by the authors, contains a whole section on incommensurate structures with several references to the structure analyses by 3D ED. Since then, the number of results increased, including, e.g. the analysis of vaterite (Steciuk et al., https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-45581-6), or recently belite (Plana-Ruiz et al., https://doi.org/10.1107/S205252062400146X).
The second, and more critical, problem is that there is very little to no information provided in the manuscript about the details of the structure determination of the incommensurate structure. While there is an extensive table provided in the SI on the refinement of all non-modulated structures (Table 2 in SI), no such table is available for the incommensurate structure – not even a refinement R-factor is provided. Furthermore, the deposited CIF files correspond only to the periodic structures, and the CIF of the modulated structure is not available. Thus, the only information on the structure is the two videos, which are not sufficient and, upon inspection, they rather raise doubts about the correctness of the structure. The expected main modulation would be the tilting of the octahedra. However, the videos show a rather chaotic variation of the oxygen positions that lead to a strong deformation of the octahedra.
Third, several points in the manuscript seem to indicate that the authors are not very familiar with the analysis of incommensurately modulated structures. One example for all: The caption to Figure 7 in SI says “Screenshot of JANA2020 in refinement of modulation vectors”. However, this screenshot shows the dialog for modulation functions, not vector.
In summary, the manuscript does not contain enough information to make it possible to check if the analysis of the incommensurately modulated phase was performed correctly, and this part needs to be significantly improved before the manuscript can be published. If the authors are not sufficiently familiar with the analysis of the modulated structures, they should seek help of an expert in the field.

### Reviewer 1

The authors have thoroughly and satisfactorily addressed all issues raised by the reviewers. I recommend the manuscript for acceptance.

### Reviewer 2

I have reviewed the revised version of the manuscript entitled In situ electron diffraction tomography study of the successive phase transitions in LaTaO4 nanocrystals. I can conclude that the authors put a lot of effort in addressing the my comments and improved the manuscript considerably.
Nevertheless, I have still identified some problems in the analysis of the modulated structure, which require some more attention. I am especially concerned by the determination of symmetry (lines 215+). The manuscript says that the observed systematic absences were of the type hk0m: h+k=2n and h0lm: l+m=2n. Then it is stated that these absences can be attributed to the superspace group Cmc21(a00)000. First of all, the first condition should be written hklm:h+k=2n, because it is induced by the centering and thus applies to all reflections, not only the h0lm subset. Second, these conditions are compatible also with the centrosymmetric space group Cmcm(a00)000. It is not explicitly stated why the non-centrosymmetric space group was selected and the centrosymmetric was not considered. I assume it is because it is known that the high-temperature phase is non-centrosymmetric. It would be good to mention this explicitly in the text. Third and most important: in the supplementary figure 7, an attempt is made to illustrate the systematic absences by circles and crosses in the h0lm section. Unfortunately, the circles and crosses in Fig. s9 are not correct. The condition h0lm: l+m=2n implies that when the main reflection is absent, the associated first-order satellites are present and vice versa. I.e., the circles and crosses form a checkerboard pattern. Please revise the figure.
Looking at the pattern in Fig. S8b and S9b, I can see a lot of violations of any possible systematic absences. The data obviously exhibit a large amount of multiple scattering - not unusual for such a simple inorganic structure. But it means that the systematic absences must be evaluated with great care. Without having access to the raw data, I cannot make a definitive verdict, but I am convinced the correct systematic absence is h0lm: l+m=2n, and the correct superspace group would then be Cmc21(a00)0s0 (or Cmcm(a00)0s0). I think that this option must be carefully evaluated before it is discarded, ideally by trying to refine a structure model in both space groups, and choosing the better model.
When reviewing the symmetry considerations for the modulated structure, I checked again also the symmetry determination of the non-modulated structures. And I am afraid the same error that might have happened in the assignment of the space group of the incommensurate structure crept in also in the analysis of the m-LaTaO4 phase. The authors argue that additional peaks are visible in the SAED patterns and in the reciprocal-space sections from the 3D ED data, disproving the P21/c space group. However, the SAED pattern shown in Fig. 1c is in an orientation that is very favourable for multiple diffraction into the reflection 00-3, and the reciprocal-space section presented in Fig. S3b shows very clear variation of intensity between the l=2n and l=2n+1 rows. Given the strong dynamical character of the data, these images are, in my opinion, consistent with the space group P21/c, and the only method of distinguising P21 and P21/c is performing the refinement in both and showing that P21 is clearly better than P21/c. But my guess is that P21/c is the better choice.
My apologies for not having spotted these problems already in the first round of revisions, but I think the problems are relatively severe and need careful consideration.

## Paper

## Abstract

The ferroelectric oxide LaTaO4, with a layered perovskite-related structure, exhibits a reversible temperature-dependent phase transition between its low-temperature paraelectric and high-temperature ferroelectric states. Herein, using in situ three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED) with atomic-resolution, we resolve the structural evolution of LaTaO4 nanocrystals across four distinct phases during sequential heating treatment (300-500 K). Beyond ab initio structure determination of the known monoclinic (m-LaTaO4) and orthorhombic (o-LaTaO4) phases, we unravel: (i) a, previously undetected, intermediate phase (m'-LaTaO4) with a shorter c-axis transiently stabilized at around 372 K, arising from tilting of TaO6 octahedra; (ii) an incommensurately modulated phase (IC-o-LaTaO4) with a modulation vector q ≈ (0.4669, 0, 0) through a combination of 3D ED and high-resolution electron microscopy imaging. The real-time tracking reveals three first-order phase transitions governed by synergetic Ta-O bond distortion dynamics. These findings establish a hierarchical phase transition model that reconciles previous studies and these single nanocrystal observations.

---

## Introduction

Ferroelectric materials1 exhibit a spontaneous net polarizationP, the direction of which is reversibly switchable under an external applied electric field. Consequently, these material s have garnered substantial interest for capacitor, sensor, actuator, and memory device applications. Ferroelectric materials can be formed via a phase transition from paraelectric phases under specific conditions, which is typically accomplished by symmetry breaking. Although the most widely-used ferroelectric materials adopt the perovskite structure, a wide range of other ferroelectrics exist within layered perovskite-like structures including Ruddlesden-Popper, Dion-Jacobson, Aurivillius and Carpy-Galy families.2,3 The latter can be derived from the perovskite (ABX3) structure by cleaving along the [110] plane and incorporation of additional anions, giving rise to the homologous series with general formula AnBnX3n+2, where n represents the number of perovskite blocks between cleaved planes. Within this Carpy-Galy4 family, the n = 4 materials Sr2Nb2O75 and La2Ti2O76,7 aroused significant attention in ferroelectric and piezoelectric research, due to their very high operating temperatures. Notably however, LaTaO48-12is the sole ferroelectric oxide n = 2 member in this family (although CeTaO4 and PrTaO4 also adopt the Carpy-Galy structure they exclusively form only in the non-polar polymorph); LaNbO4 and all other lanthanide (Ln) tantalates and niobates with ABX4 stoichiometry adopted either the non-perovskite-related fergusonite or scheelite structures.13-15 LaTaO4 is of particular interest as it shares structural similarities with the prototypical ferroelectric fluoride analogue, BaMnF4,16 which exhibits a stable nonpolar monoclinic P21/c phase (m-phase) at room temperature and a stable polar orthorhombic Cmc21 phase at high temperature.17,18 In previous studies of the phase transitions of LaTaO4,17,19 an incommensurately modulated structure was identified between the low temperature m-phase and the high temperature o-phase, accompanied by dielectric anomalies during heating and cooling.

Previous studies on crystal structures and phase transitions of LaTaO4 mainly rely on powder X-ray or neutron diffraction.8,20 However, three-dimensional reciprocal information was projected to one dimension in these techniques, leading to peak overlaps and potential oversight of subtle reflection signals in background noises. These limitations hinder differentiation between similar structures and increase the risk of missing key features. Three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED)21,22 is an emerging method developed in the past two decades, which has been applied to structure analysis of various materials including inorganic minerals, proteins, crystalline porous materials, etc.23-26 In particular, in situ 3D ED affords the capability of probing not only crystal structures under various environments, e.g. cryogenic temperatures, electric fields, in situ heating, and in gas and liquid environments, but also the dynamic structure evolution under external stimuli.27-29

Here, we utilised in situ 3D ED to track the successive phase transitions of LaTaO4 nanocrystals during thermal cycling. The temperature-dependent structural evolution was resolved through the analysis of 3D reciprocal lattices. In addition to the three previously reported phases, a previously unreported intermediate monoclinic phase, denoted as m'-LaTaO4 phase, was identified between the monoclinic and incommensurate orthorhombic phases in some nanocrystals. Through ab initio structural solutions, we characterised all crystalline phases and established their relationships. By combining 3D ED data with high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) imaging, we elucidated the incommensurate modulation structure including its modulation vector, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of various atomic-level structures in LaTaO4.

In this work, the typical crystal structures of m-LaTaO4 (a = 7.67 Å, b = 5.67 Å, and c = 7.94 Å, β = 101.57°, space group P21/c) and o-LaTaO4 (a = 4.05 Å, b = 15.11 Å, and c = 5.80 Å, space group Cmc21) were successfully determined using 3D ED data (Supplementary Fig. 1 and 2 and Supplementary Table 1). To investigate the phase transition behaviour of LaTaO4 during progressive heating, an in situ heating 3D ED experiment was carefully designed and conducted (Fig. 1), so that 3D ED datasets were collected at preset temperatures with a fixed heating rate of 5 K/min (Fig. 1a) from multiple LaTaO4 nanocrystals (Fig. 1b), followed by an equilibration period of 5 mins at each temperature.

3D ED datasets (Fig. 2a-c) were firstly collected at 300 K, from which a monoclinic unit cell with parameters a = 7.63 Å, b = 5.63 Å, and c = 7.92 Å, β = 101.09° was determined, consistent with previously reported m-LaTaO4. However, analysis of 2D slices from the 3D ED data revealed the presence of numerous diffraction spots with h0l (l = 2n+1), which contradicts the systematic absences expected for the widely reported space group P21/c. Given the composition of heavy atoms (La, Ta) and the high density, this observation is likely attributed to strong dynamical scattering effects. This interpretation is supported by a consistent intensity difference observed between h0l reflections with l = 2n and l = 2n+1 indices. From a property perspective, the assignment of the centrosymmetric P21/c space group remains consistent with the well-documented paraelectric behaviour of m-LaTaO4. The observed reflection conditions were summarised as h0l: l = 2n; 00l: l = 2n; 0k0: k = 2n, shown in Supplementary Fig. 3. During heating, SAED patterns along a fixed orientation of the same crystal were recorded with 0.5 s exposure time. Representative SAED patterns at 360, 380 and 400 K are shown in Fig. 1c-e. At 360 K, SAED patterns displayed sharp diffraction spots from both zero-order Laue zone (ZOLZ) and first-order Laue zone (FOLZ), indexed to the [1̅20] of m-LaTaO4. It is worth noting that some diffraction spots, such as 003 and 003̅, should be systematically absent based on the reported space group P21/c but weak spots are present in the experimental SAED pattern (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 4). This indicates the existence of strong dynamical scattering, which corroborates with the emergence of h0l (l = 2n+1) reflections in 3D ED datasets.

A line profile was extracted from the diffraction pattern along (001̅) direction (marked by the dotted yellow rectangle in Fig. 1c-e), from 214 to 216̅ reflections (Fig. 1f). By recording SAED patterns along the identical orientation of the same nanocrystal during heating, the evolution of diffraction spots could be tracked (Supplementary Video 1 and 2). Fig. 1g and h show the change in intensity of the reflections shown in Fig. 1f during the heating with an interval of 1 K. No obvious change was observed from 300 to 368 K. In this range of temperature, the unit cells determined from 3D ED datasets remain the same as m-LaTaO4. When temperature was increased to approx. 372 K, the nanocrystal underwent a first change. In the range 368 ~ 380 K, the intensities of strong diffraction spots display a visible fluctuation at around 372 K and gradually stabilize at 380 K. Moreover, the 216̅ reflection (marked with an arrow in Fig. 1g) shows a slight shift. Subsequent 3D ED data analysis at 380 K showed significant intensity reduction in h0l (l ≠ 2n) reflections versus room-temperature data (Supplementary Fig. 5). Since two 3D ED datasets are collected from the same particle, the changes in reflection intensities and positions indicate a potential phase transition.

It is worth noting that the changes in intensity of many other reflections are not so prominent. After careful analysis of the 3D ED dataset at 380 K, a monoclinic phase with parameters a = 7.78 Å, b = 5.65 Å, c = 3.97 Å, and β = 100.94° with a space group of P21 could be determined, denoted as m'-LaTaO4 (Fig. 2d-f). However, this intermediate m'-phase is not very stable and only appears in a narrow temperature range. In many cases, m- and m'-phases might coexist in LaTaO4 nanocrystals. Notably, the m'-phase exhibits such subtle structural differences that it remains undetectable in conventional powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) and neutron diffraction (PND). This limitation arises from two fundamental factors: Firstly, the pronounced overlap of diffraction peaks between the m- and m'-phases leads to statistical averaging of their respective signals in PXRD/PND patterns, effectively obscuring the weaker m'-phase signatures during analysis. Secondly, the m'-LaTaO4 likely exists only at the nanoscale or within localised structural domains, making it inherently challenging to observe through other characterisation techniques.

As the temperature continues to increase from 380 K, the intensities of diffraction spots remain stable until the second phase transition occurs, from the m'-phase to IC-o phase, at ca. 389 K. In addition to changes in reflection intensities, the positions of 214 and 214̅ reflections also shift (marked with yellow arrows in Fig. 1h). Analysis of in situ 3D ED data at 400 K reveals an orthorhombic unit cell with incommensurate modulation (Fig. 2g-i), where the basic cell parameters (a = 3.95 Å, b = 14.58 Å and c = 5.69 Å) agree well with the reported o-LaTaO4. Distinct ‘zig-zag’ satellite spots appear along the (001) direction with a modulation vector q ≈ (0.4669, 0, 0) in 3D reciprocal space, consistent with the previous study by Howieson et al.17

As the temperature continues to increase to ca. 394 ~ 400 K, the diffraction pattern shows a final change, with variations in reflection intensity only (Fig. 1e). Subsequent 3D ED data (Fig. 2j-l) confirms the formation of the high-temperature orthorhombic phase, o-LaTaO4. The unit cell parameters could be determined as a = 3.92 Å, b = 14.41 Å and c = 5.61 Å (at 500 K), with the space group Cmc21. Notably, these phase transition temperatures (389 or 394 K) are lower than widely-reported ones (~ 440 K8,17). Given the non- negligible volume changes among different phases, from 333.61 Å3 (m-LaTaO4 @300 K), 335.76 Å3 (2×m'-LaTaO4 @380 K), 327.52 Å3 (IC-o-LaTaO4 @400 K) to 316.32 Å3 (o-LaTaO4 @500 K), a possible origin of the change in transition temperatures (Tc) value is strain, that the expansion in unit cell volume during heating may have effect on lattice strains, resulting in a decrease of Tc. The dependence of Tc on unit cell volume have been reported in perovskite such as LaCoO330 And the Tc of ferroelectric (CnH2n+1NH3)2(CH3NH3)n-1PbnBr3n+1 could be decreased by the expansion of unit cells.31 Another possible answer could be the size effect of nanoparticles. Zhong et al.32 hypothesised and validated that Tc would drop as the size of ferroelectric nanoparticles decreases using a Landau phenomenological theory. Lyberatos et al.33 proposed that the Curie temperature of L1o-FePt would decrease as the size decreases based on simulations using a Monte Carlo model.

Structure analysis of LaTaO4 phases

In situ 3D ED datasets of all phases (m-LaTaO4, m'-LaTaO4, IC-o-LaTaO4 (main reflections)and o-LaTaO4) were processed using XDS34 software. Ab initio structure solutions were obtained using direct methods in SIR2019,35 followed by structure refinements using SHELXL36 in OLEX237. Crystallographic details of selected 3D ED datasets at 300, 340, 380, 400, 440, 480 and 500 K are provided in Supplementary Table 2. Structural comparisons of m-LaTaO4, m'-LaTaO4 and IC-o-LaTaO4 (Fig. 3) reveal that, apart from minor La position variations, the main difference of these structures lies in the arrangement of twin TaO6 octahedral blocks (TO). In the m-phase, TaO6 octahedra exhibit an overall out-of-phase tilt around [001]m while in both the m'- and o-phases the octahedral tilting is in-phase along the equivalent axis, [001]m' and [100]o, respectively. As a result, m-LaTaO4 has two types of twin TaO6 octahedra stacked alternately, TOm1 and TOm2 (marked with arrows), along the [001] (or [100]o) direction whilst m'-LaTaO4 and o-LaTaO4 have only one type (TOm' and TOo respectively). The measured angles of Ta–O–Ta (Δθ) in these structures show deviations from 180° (the un-tilted parent Cmcm structure): ΔθTOm1 = 38.462°, ΔθTOm2 = -38.462°, ΔθTOm' = 35.54° and ΔθTOo = 33.34°, respectively (the absolute value of ΔθTOm1 and ΔθTOm2 are equal because of the c-centring symmetry of P21/c). This progressive Δθ change indicates that from m-LaTaO4 to m'-LaTaO4, the TO6 octahedra rotate, with one TaO6 block TOm2 rotating anticlockwise, and the other block TOm1 rotating clockwise, resulting in the alignment of TOm' and TOm' along [001]m. And the overall transition from m-LaTaO4 to o-LaTaO4 has the tendency to a higher degree of octahedral alignment towards an ideal (un-tilted) Cmcm structure. This trend is corroborated by temperature-dependent Δθ analysis (Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 3). Data merging could improve the data completeness but shows little changes on the structure refinement statistics in our cases (Supplementary Table 4).

Regarding the phase transformation from m'-LaTaO4 to IC-o-LaTaO4, a comparison between m'-LaTaO4 and the averaged IC-o-LaTaO4 was conducted, as illustrated in Fig. 3b. Differences could be seen along [010]m', where no obvious rotations of TaO6 octahedra could be identified, but an overall shift of the n = 2 TaO6 layers and La ions along the [001] direction was found. Although the shift is small, ca. 0.36a of the unit cell (~ 1.44 Å), it induces the alignment of La and TaO6 blocks along the [010] direction, resulting in an orthogonal arrangement that drives the structure to a different phase of LaTaO4.

However, mere consideration of only the main reflections does not completely represent the exact structure of IC-o-LaTaO4 as satellite spots were excluded in the structure determination. To further investigate the superstructures, multiple datasets of m'-LaTaO4 and IC-o-LaTaO4 from several repeated experiments were analysed. For IC-o-LaTaO4, accounting for weak diffraction spots revealed an incommensurately modulated supercell along the a-axis. The q vectors from all IC-o-LaTaO4 phases have been determined and summarised (Supplementary Table 5). Furthermore, after introducing a modulation vector in data processing of 3D ED datasets using PETS2 (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 7a),38 the intensity of satellite spots could be integrated, generating a (3+1)D reflection file rather than a standard hkl file. The 0th slices of IC-o-LaTaO4 in hk0m and h0lm are shown in Supplementary Fig. 8. The first-order satellites could be seen in the IC-o-LaTaO4 dataset, but second-order satellite spots are absent, hence only m = 1 is considered. Similarly, the reflections suffer from strong dynamical scattering, by considering the variation of reflection conditions, the reflection conditions could be summarised as hklm: h+k = 2n, and h0lm: l+m = 2n. The reflection conditions are compatible with superspace group Cmc21(α00)0s0, C2cm(α00)ss0 (Ama2(00g)0ss in the standard setting) and Cmcm(α00)0s0. Cmcm(α00)0s0 was excluded, as its basic space group Cmcm is centrosymmetric, which is incompatible with the widely reported ferroelectricity nature of the high temperature LaTaO4 phase.8,9 For the non-centrosymmetric alternatives, C2cm(α00)ss0 was not selected because its symmetry forbids the modulation of z, which precludes any modulated displacement functions along z in the incommensurately modulated model. Such constraints are incompatible with the tilting-dominated incommensurate modulation. In addition, the C2cm symmetry would impose strict constraints on the local atomic geometry. Therefore, the non-centrosymmetric space group Cmc21(α00)0s0 is selected for the incommensurate modulation. The reflection condition with index could be seen in Supplementary Fig. 9. The structure refinement workflow contains: (1) ab initio solution and refinement using only main reflections; (2) reprocessing reflection data including satellite spots; (3) kinematical structure refinement in JANA202039 by introducing a modulation vector q = (0.4669, 0, 0) and superspace group Cmc21(α00)0s0 (Supplementary Fig. 7b). The refinement statistics are summarised in Supplementary Table 6. The finalised model could be seen in Fig. 4b and c, and the de Wolff sections could be seen in Supplementary Fig. 10.

In the refined incommensurately modulated superstructure model of IC-o-LaTaO4, Ta, O and La atoms exhibit positional variations, resulting in a tilting of TaO6 octahedra and a minor displacement of La (Supplementary Video 3 and 4). The tilting of TaO6 is accompanied by minor deformations, which does not appear to be symmetry-dictated. To give a clear presentation, we built a superstructure model with 22×a (Fig. 4d), in which two types of TaO6 blocks with different orientations were identified. These blocks are alternatively connected and exhibit subtle differences in oxygen displacement magnitude, with variations manifesting a long-range modulation period. To display this structural feature, a colour contrast gradient is introduced in Fig. 4d depending on the extent of oxygen position variation. As the oxygen atoms vary in their positions, there are always regions where unit cells of type A and B show more similar structures. This similarity is followed by a gradual deviation between two types until reaching regions with maximum structural difference. However, if we further extend the scale of the model, one can easily find that the periods are not commensurate. This is where the incommensurate modulation originates. This principle aligns with the formation mechanism of incommensurate structures proposed in our previous study, i.e. that the partial ordering of two or more different blocks is the origin for the formation of the incommensurate structures.17

JANA software has been widely used to determine incommensurately modulated crystal structures, mainly utilizing powder or single-crystal X-ray diffraction and powder neutron diffraction data.40-43 In common cases, electron microscopy primarily provides SAED and HRTEM images from limited orientations. Recently, more exemplar research has been reported on the structure refinement of incommensurately modulated structures using 3D ED, PED, etc.21,44-47 Building upon the ongoing development of 3D ED methodologies, this work presents a further application case, demonstrating its utility for refining an incommensurately modulated structure upon in situ heating scenario. Notably, 3D ED has exhibited a strong capability in identifying modulated structures by offering the advantage of not only free rotation in 3D reciprocal space but also accurate indexing during determining the modulation vectors. Conventionally, determining modulation vectors through either real space or reciprocal space by electron microscopy is usually time-consuming and lacks accuracy. This is because structure modulation determination requires a large number of images taken from different orientations, all of which require accurate indexing prior to satellite spots analysis. Furthermore, SAED patterns represent 2D sections of reciprocal space. The interpretation of satellite spots or weak superlattice reflections could be insufficient due to its limited orientation, making it difficult in correctly determining the incommensurate modulation or other superstructures in these materials. In contrast, 3D ED datasets provide structural information in 3D reciprocal space, enabling unrestricted rotation of reconstructed 3D data and 2D section until the correct modulation vector is identified. In addition, with the exploitation of data processing software, e.g. PETS2,38 the modulation vectors can be reliably determined and refined.

The incommensurate structure was further confirmed through high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) imaging. Fig. 5a-d shows a representative HRTEM image taken along the [001]o direction with its corresponding fast Fourier transform (FFT) pattern and electron diffraction pattern. Analysis of satellite spots observed in the FFT and electron diffraction gives the modulation vector q ≈ (0.4624, 0, 0), which is close to that from 3D ED data (0.4669, 0, 0). A line profile along the [100]o direction (Fig. 5e) reveals prominent intensity variations superimposed on the periodic lattice fringes. Two distinct periods exhibiting wave-like modulations are identified (marked in blue for period 1 and red for period 2 in Fig. 5e). By selecting main Fourier coefficients or satellites in the FFT data and performing inverse Fourier transformation, two different images were obtained (middle and bottom left in Fig. 5e). The corresponding line profile (blue curve in Fig. 5e) of only the main reflections presents an overall even distribution whilst the line profile of the satellite reflections (red curve in Fig. 5e) resembles a harmonic wave, with a ca. 6.5×a period. This abnormal contrast difference originates from atomic-scale structural modulations involving La atomic displacements and cooperative TaO6 octahedra tilting. Moreover, HRTEM observations show good agreement with the proposed structure model (Supplementary Fig. 11), that alternating type A and type B domains exhibit characteristic contrast variations over extended length scales. From the full scale filtered HRTEM images with the FFTs in Supplementary Fig. 12, the wavelike patterns, which indicate the incommensuration in the LaTaO4 structure, are distributed across the whole specimen area.

As a sequential work following the study of IC-o-LaTaO4 carried out by Howieson et al.,17 a comparison with the current work can be made. While no unit cell can be strictly defined for incommensurate structures, an expanded supercell with ordered building blocks (“slabs”) approaching the incommensurate structure serves as a conceptual framework for understanding structure formation.48,49 Unlike the “slab” incommensurate model, which assumes partial ordering of building blocks M (6×a/2) and N (5×a/2) based on SAED and HRTEM observations, this work constructs a single-crystal-level structural description. Specifically, we propose a structure model with quantified atomic position approximation rather than “slab” subunit hypothesis. Meanwhile, differing from conventional refinement of a standard database structure using PND data, this study conducted ab initio structure solution, together with structure refinement using 3D ED data, enabling improved approximation of local structural realism.

Nonetheless, despite the differences, the models in the current work are not at odds with those previously reported, but instead complement the understanding of the incommensurate modulation in LaTaO4. The modulation vector q of IC-o-LaTaO4 is close to the reported vector (0.456, 0, 0), exhibiting consistent SAED patterns along the [001]o direction. HRTEM images reveal two alternating intensity periods with wave-like characteristics (top right in Fig. 5e), suggesting that at least two building blocks contribute to the modulated structure in LaTaO4. It is important to note that both “slab” and our models are approximations of the real structure, as satellite spot intensity arises from atomic displacements across hundreds of unit cells.

Overall, the benefits of in situ heating 3D ED reflect in many extents, that upon progressive heating, it is possible to track the crystal structure evolution and obtain a realistic structure under different environments, effectively capturing phase transition behaviour of LaTaO4 nanocrystals. Moreover, the rapid 3D ED data collection makes it possible to detect subtle changes in structures, enabling discovery of transient phases such as the potential intermediate phase, m'-LaTaO4. In this work, the phase transitions and structural evolution of LaTaO4 were investigated using in situ 3D ED coupled with HRTEM imaging. Upon heating the specimen from 300 K to 500 K, the monoclinic phase (m-LaTaO4) underwent a phase transition to an intermediate phase (m'-LaTaO4) at approximately 372 K. Such a phase transition involves a tilting of TO6 blocks to align with TOm1, generating the intermediate phase structurally analogous to m-LaTaO4 but with a unit cell halved in c. Subsequently, the octahedral layers undergo a shift along the [001]m' direction during the transition to an incommensurately modulated orthorhombic phase (IC-o-LaTaO4) with a modulation along the a-axis and a modulation vector q ≈ (0.4669, 0, 0). A final transition at approximately 394 K yielded the fully ordered orthorhombic phase (o-LaTaO4). The crystal structures of m-LaTaO4, m'-LaTaO4 and the averaged IC-o-LaTaO4 phases were resolved ab initio. Based on 3D ED data and HRTEM image analysis, an incommensurately modulated model of IC-o-LaTaO4 was proposed. The methodology demonstrated in the present work enables investigation of phase transitions with subtle structural changes in many other solid materials.

## Methods

Material Synthesis

The m-LaTaO4 specimen was prepared as a polycrystalline powder according to previous literature17 and used as prepared without further purification. A standard synthesis procedure involves: Reagents are dried for 1 hour before use—La2O3 at 1000 °C and Ta2O5 at 600 °C. Stoichiometric quantities of the oxides are mixed via milling at 600 rpm for 1 hour in a planetary ball mill, then pressed into pellets 10 ~ 13 mm in diameter using either 1 tonne uniaxial pressure or 200 MPa isostatic pressure. The pellets are subsequently annealed at 1650 °C for 6 hours.

In situ heating 3D ED experiment

Sample preparation. The original m-LaTaO4 specimen was used in the in situ heating experiment. The sample was crushed and dispersed in anhydrous ethanol. The dispersed sample was dropped onto an in situ chip (Fusion Select by Protochips Co. Ltd.) with a 3×3 mesh and left to allow the complete evaporation of ethanol. It should be noted that the amount of dispersed sample was low to avoid blocking of the mesh apertures.

In situ system setup. The heating procedure was controlled by an in situ heating system, which consists of a heater, an in situ specimen holder (Fusion Select: E-FHDC-VO) and a controlling terminal (controlling software Fusion installed in a PC). The in situ holder was connected to the heater and the controlling terminal. The software checks the connection between in situ chip, heater and the controlling system, and the ‘pass’ feedback indicates the in situ system is ready to perform the experiment. For each in situ chip, a calibration file was provided by the manufacturer in order to calibrate the controller electricity parameters under different temperatures and ramping rates. The calibration file was imported to the controlling software before experiment.

TEM setup. The in situ experiment was performed on JEOL JEM-F200 microscope with an ASI Cheetah 1800 camera and a RIO-16 camera. The microscope, with an acceleration voltage of 200 kV, was aligned before experiment.

In situ heating 3D ED experiment design. The temperature was set to 300 K at the beginning of experiment, then increased with a constant rate of 5 K/min, and paused at 300, 340, 380, 400, 440, 480 and finally 500 K to collect 3D ED data (Figure 1). Temperature stabilization for ca. 5 mins was applied before 3D ED data collection. One single crystal was tracked and its SAED patterns were recorded during the heating procedure.

In situ 3D ED data collection. The in situ 3D ED datasets were collected using the ASI-Cheetah 1800 camera combined with a modified INSTAMATIC data collection software.22,28,50 The continuous rotation electron diffraction (cRED) method was used in data collection and an exposure time of either 0.3 s or 0.5 s was used. Due to the dimension of holder, the collection range was -25 ~ 25°.

HRTEM imaging. HRTEM images were taken with a Gatan RIO-16 detector equipped on a JEOL JEM-F200 transmission electron microscope, operating at 200 kV.

Data processing, structural solution and refinement

3D ED reconstruction. The data processing was performed using PETS238 software, including signal extraction and 3D reconstruction. The reflection diameter for peak search is 10 pixels and I/sigma for 20. The original modulated vector was determined and refined as q = (0.4669, 0.0028, -0.0006). The LaTaO4 phases were recognised, their unit cells and the superspace groups were determined using the reconstructed 3D ED data and reciprocal sections generated by PETS2. The frame geometry and reflection profile were also optimised before integration.

Intensity integration. The intensity integration of diffraction spots was conducted by an XDS software for ab initio structural solution. For the incommensurate phase, the determined unit cell and space group were imported into XDS to extract the diffraction information for structural solution of the basic unit cell and refinement of the periodic crystal structure. Besides, data with the modulation vector with maximum satellite order of 1 were integrated and finalised using an integrate profile for intensity estimation in PETS2 in order to refine the modulated structure.

Structural solution and refinement. The initial structural solutions of m-LaTaO4, m'-LaTaO4 and o-LaTaO4 were obtained using direct methods in SIR201935 and refined using a SHELXL36 program in OLEX237. The averaged structure of IC-o-LaTaO4 was also obtained by this means. To gain an incommensurately modulated structure, a satellite-containing (3+1)D reflection file processed by PETS2 was imported to the refinement of the averaged IC-o-LaTaO4 structure using JANA202039. A least-squares method was used for refinement.

The manuscript “In situ electron diffraction tomography unveils sequential phase transitions in LaTaO₄ nanocrystals” by Wu et al. reports on an electron diffraction-based structural study of intermediate phases emerging during the thermal evolution of LaTaO₄. In principle, the authors could use this data to outline a phase transition path on a PT phase diagram within the low-pressure region. The study is solid, and the main message of the paper is clear. I generally liked the paper and recommend it for publication.
I have a few minor remarks:
- I strongly recommend depositing the original data in a public repository (e.g., Zenodo) and including a static link to the data in the manuscript.
- For such small tilt ranges, was crystal tracking by defocusing the diffraction pattern really necessary?
- Was any data merging performed to mitigate issues related to poor completeness?

3-2 For such small tilt ranges, was crystal tracking by defocusing the diffraction pattern really
necessary?
RESPONSE: Indeed, in small tilting angles (e.g. ≤ 30°), the specimen drift is not dramatic, and it
is not necessary for defocusing during data collection if the whole microcrystal is within the
selected-area aperture. However, tracking specimen through defocusing is still a safer way,
especially for 3D ED data collection from local regions (tip of rods, corner of crystals, etc.), or edges
in relatively large crystals (ED data quality may be bad in central area of large crystals). We might
not be able to illuminate the same region without crystal tracking.
